Some of these shrines are also called '''Jūnishō''' (十二社). 

These shrines can be categorized into two main types:
1. Shrines dedicated to local mountain deities called '''Jūni-sama''' (Twelve Lords), associated with ancient rituals and the customs of the "Twelve Lectures." These shrines are primarily found in mountainous areas of eastern Japan, especially in the northern {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|qid=Q132480|lt=Kantō region}} and {{ill|Kōshin'etsu region|en|Kōshin'etsu region|qid=Q398208|lt=Kōshin'etsu region}}. Research indicates that 65% of the 438 shrines named Jūnisho or Jūnisha enshrine {{ill|Ōyamatsumi|en|Ōyamatsumi|qid=Q386563|qid=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi}} as their main deity.
2. Shrines that enshrine the {{ill|Kumano shrine|ja|熊野三山|lt=Kumano Sanzan}} deities (known as {{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現}}). These were originally called '''Jūnisho Gongen-sha'''. During the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, many of these shrines modified their enshrined deities to the "{{ill|Kamiyonanayo|ja|天神七代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heavenly Generations Seven|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神世七代|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q3275893}}" and "{{ill|Five Generations of Earth Deities|ja|地神五代|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Earthly Generations Five|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q18337308}}," or the "Twelve Gods of the Heavenly Generation."
